report:
**Conclusion:** Yes, offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) significantly increases overall HIV testing uptake compared to relying solely on standard HIV testing services.

### Evidence Summary

Multiple systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) confirm that making HIV self-testing available increases the proportion of people who get tested:

* **General Population Gains:** A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 RCTs showed that offering HIVST doubled the uptake of HIV testing in the general population across various delivery models and support tools (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext).
* **Key Populations:** A systematic review of 10 RCTs focusing on key populations found that distributing free HIV self-testing kits increased HIV testing uptake compared to standard care across all subgroup analyses (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z).
* **WHO Guidance Support:** A systematic review conducted to inform World Health Organization guidelines concluded there is moderate-quality evidence that HIVST increases HIV testing uptake, alongside low-quality evidence that it increases testing frequency (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.7448/IAS.20.1.21594).
* **Direct Demand Increase:** Individual randomized controlled trials further demonstrate that promoting and providing self-test options directly increases testing demand and overall testing rates (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10461-018-2248-5).

By overcoming common barriers associated with standard facility-based care—such as privacy concerns, stigma, and access limitations—the additional offer of HIV self-testing successfully leads to higher testing participation.
